weeks.title: On Work
weeks.poemCredit: Kahlil Gibran (1883 to 1931), "On Work" (1923). Public domain. Source: Project Gutenberg (The Prophet, eBook #58585, Kahlil Gibran).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: a woman at a spinning wheel, Sogn og Fjordane, Norway, early 1900s. Fylkesarkivet i Sogn og Fjordane. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
Kahlil Gibran (1883 to 1931) published The Prophet in 1923, and a century on, his chapter "On Work" still reframes the most ordinary tasks. To weave, to build, to sow, all of it done as if for someone you love. The poem asks us to treat the day's labor as a form of tenderness. A quiet place to begin.

weeks.title: Song of the Broad-Axe
weeks.poemCredit: Walt Whitman (1819 to 1892), "Song of the Broad-Axe" (1856). Public domain. Source: Project Gutenberg, Leaves of Grass by Walt Whitman (eBook #1322).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: a ship-carpenter's workshop, Altonaer Museum, Hamburg. Christoph Braun (CC0).
weeks.caption:
Walt Whitman (1819 to 1892) wrote "Song of the Broad-Axe" in 1856, and he lets one tool summon the whole shape of a life. The same axe yields the coffin and the bride's bed, the babe's cradle and the floor-planks under the dancers' feet, the roof over the supper at day's end. The word "shape" runs back to the Old English scieppan, to create or ordain; here the made thing and the act of making are the same gesture. Every room we live inside was once measured and joined by someone's hands.

weeks.title: The Solitary Reaper
weeks.poemCredit: William Wordsworth (1770 to 1850), "The Solitary Reaper" (1807). Public domain. Source: Wikisource: Poems, in Two Volumes (Wordsworth, 1807), Volume 2, "The solitary Reaper" (first-publication text).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: Dorothea Lange, field worker, San Joaquin Valley, California, 1938. FSA, Library of Congress. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
William Wordsworth (1770 to 1850) watched a Highland girl bend to her sickle in 1807, singing in a tongue he could not understand, and he never forgot the sound. He stopped, listened until he had his fill, and carried the music up the hill long after the field had gone quiet behind him. The word "reaper" comes from the Old English ripan, to gather what has ripened; she gathers grain, and he gathers song. What he keeps on the climb is the music, borne in the heart after it is heard no more. The work ends; the song goes on with him.

weeks.title: Coromandel Fishers
weeks.poemCredit: Sarojini Naidu (1879 to 1949), "Coromandel Fishers" (1905). Public domain. Source: Project Gutenberg, "The Golden Threshold" by Sarojini Naidu (eBook #680), plain-text edition; cross-checked against Wikisource.
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: harbour at Svolvær, Nordland, Norway, c. 1900. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
Sarojini Naidu (1879 to 1949) wrote "Coromandel Fishers" in 1905, and it opens as a summons across the surf: rise, brothers, the wind asleep in the arms of the dawn like a child that has cried all night. The fishers gather their nets, set the catamarans free, and row out for the leaping wealth of the tide. What stays with me is the kinship she draws: the sea their mother, the cloud their brother, the waves their comrades. Work as something a whole crew rises for together, under the same pale gold light.

weeks.title: The Song of the Shirt
weeks.poemCredit: Thomas Hood (1799 to 1845), "The Song of the Shirt" (1843). Public domain. Source: Project Gutenberg, The Poetical Works of Thomas Hood (ebook 15652).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: Lewis Hine, garment workers, Upper East Side, New York, c. 1912. National Child Labor Committee, Library of Congress. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
Thomas Hood (1799 to 1845) wrote "The Song of the Shirt" in 1843, giving voice to a seamstress sewing by candlelight in poverty and cold. Her cry turns the cloth into an accusation: the thread wears down a human life as surely as it wears the linen. Stitch, stitch, stitch, a double thread that makes a shroud as readily as a shirt. The verb to manufacture once meant made by hand, and Hood keeps that hand in view, hungry and tired and real. Behind the cheapest thing is always someone's hours.

weeks.title: We Wear the Mask
weeks.poemCredit: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872 to 1906), "We Wear the Mask" (1895). Public domain. Source: Academy of American Poets (Poets.org).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: portrait of a young man, from W. E. B. Du Bois's American Negro exhibit at the 1900 Paris Exposition. Library of Congress. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872 to 1906) wrote "We Wear the Mask" in 1895, the son of formerly enslaved parents giving voice to a face arranged for the world's comfort. The mask grins and lies; it hides the cheeks and shades the eyes, and beneath it the heart is torn and still smiling. So much of any working day asks for this quiet labor of composure, a cost the room never sees. "Why should the world be over-wise, in counting all our tears and sighs?" A poem to hold gently.

weeks.title: Invictus
weeks.poemCredit: William Ernest Henley (1849 to 1903), "Invictus" (1888). Public domain. Source: Academy of American Poets (Poets.org).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: rough sea at Bognor, Sussex, England. Detroit Publishing Co., c. 1899. Library of Congress. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
William Ernest Henley (1849 to 1903) wrote "Invictus" in 1888 from a hospital bed, recovering from the tuberculosis of the bone that had already cost him a leg. The word is Latin for "unconquered," and the poem earns it slowly: the wrath and tears, the menace of the years, the strait gate and the charged scroll, all named before that final couplet arrives. What the poem holds onto is small and unkillable: a command over how you meet things, while the things themselves stay outside your reach. Mastery of fate, captaincy of the soul. A steadying thing to carry into hard, uncertain work.

weeks.title: Weaving
weeks.poemCredit: Lucy Larcom (1824 to 1893), "Weaving" (1869). Public domain. Source: Wikisource, Poems (Larcom), 1869 edition (Fields, Osgood, & Co.); transcribed from the original page scans (Page:Poems_Larcom.djvu/150). Opening corroborated by Poetry Foundation and Poetry Nook; closing stanza corroborated by the AmericanStudier blog.
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: a weaver at her loom, Paterson, New Jersey. Lewis Hine, 1937. U.S. National Archives, WPA National Research Project. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
Lucy Larcom (1824 to 1893) began work in the Lowell textile mills as a child, and "Weaving" (1869) carries the loom into the poem: the woof strong, the warp good, the day measured by the shuttle's pass. She names the plain reasons for the labor, to be her mother's stay and to win her daily food. Then the work opens outward, and "the world of women haunteth me," each one bent over some loom of her own. The word "stay" once meant a support that holds a thing upright. A length of cloth, and the lives held inside its threads.

weeks.title: And did those feet in ancient time
weeks.poemCredit: William Blake (1757 to 1827), "And did those feet in ancient time" (c. 1808). Public domain. Source: American Literature (americanliterature.com).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: the mill district of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Jack Delano, 1940. Library of Congress, FSA/OWI Collection. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
William Blake (1757 to 1827) wrote these lines around 1808, in the preface to his epic Milton, while the first mills of industrial England were darkening the valleys. The images run hot: a bow of burning gold, arrows of desire, a chariot of fire, a sword that will not sleep. Blake calls it "mental fight," the long and unglamorous labor of building something worthy of the green land it stands on. Jerusalem here is a city to be made by hand, in this place, by this work. The forge stays lit because the building is still unfinished.

weeks.title: I Hear America Singing
weeks.poemCredit: Walt Whitman (1819 to 1892), "I Hear America Singing" (1860). Public domain. Source: Academy of American Poets (Poets.org).
weeks.photoCredit: Photograph: Power house mechanic working on a steam pump. Lewis Hine, 1920. U.S. National Archives. Public domain.
weeks.caption:
Walt Whitman (1819 to 1892) heard a whole country at work and turned it into a chorus, each trade with a song of its own. The mason, the shoemaker, the mother at her labor, the wood-cutter at noon. What I love here is the dignity of the particular: each person singing the song that is theirs alone. One country, and a chorus made of separate songs.
